people.ben: Builds Heatmap with Claude and owns the page.
people.Henry: Leads the thermal management roadmap in MTC's Engineering Design team. The person Heatmap is for.
people.Claude: Does the searching, building and writing up.

entries.title: Kickoff with Henry
entries.summary: ben and Henry framed the problem in a recorded conversation, then answered Claude's planning questions together and watched Heatmap V1 go live with 25 cards.
entries.time_note: The recorded discussion came first and its start time wasn't noted. The times shown are the planning and build session that followed, up to ben's mood-board request.
discussed: Henry leads MTC's new thermal management roadmap in the Engineering Design team. It is the first year, so it starts from a blank sheet, and he has little time for it.
MTC capabilities to match against: additive manufacturing (the biggest), laser processes, robotics, metrology and inspection, modelling and simulation, and design for manufacture.

The target is the middle of a Venn diagram: a societal or industrial problem (ideally a UK one), a thermal management technology (new, or existing but not yet applied) and an MTC capability. Plus the organisations worth talking to, where small companies are often the most interesting.

The existing MTC tool ranks poorly and misses papers whose uses are only implied. Good example: a Danish RTO's printed thermosiphon cold plate for data centres. Bad example: a replacement speedboat intercooler.
Ideas raised: an interactive page that experts give feedback to and that learns, a monthly snapshot report, and a quick way to feed in notes from industry conversations.
Constraints: V1 is built outside MTC IT with public data only. A company-hosted version would later need locally hosted models and data provenance.
decided: Henry is the only V1 user. Feedback is a vote plus an optional "why".
It runs daily on ben's Claude subscription and publishes to a shared Claude page, with code and data in a private GitHub repo.
Henry's requirements document is inspiration only, and nobody else needs to approve V1.
A notes box for non-confidential notes from industry chats is in scope. Trade press and UK and EU research and RTO news come first.
Claude leads with its own judgement. Henry's 10 calibration examples are a sanity check, not a target.
Three areas built together: data-centre cooling, aerospace heat exchangers (cabin-air precoolers and turbofan oil coolers) and F1 thermal management.
Widen the search with technology-first and research searches (agreed at 18:48; the sweep ran just after the meeting).
built: The Heatmap V1 plan, with the calibration set and an acceptance test.
The private repo bentillettai/heatmap, created by ben.
Heatmap V1, live at 18:39 with 25 cards from 64 articles, and the daily run scheduled for 06:59.

entries.title: Wider search sweep
entries.summary: The sweep agreed at the end of the meeting: 65 more articles read, 12 new cards, 37 in total.
items: Honeywell's £14.1M STRATA cabin-air project now covers part of the precooler gap.
New motorsport cards on Dallara and Conflux's liquid-hydrogen evaporator and on student race-car cooling.
Six cards from searching by technology first, such as laser-textured boiling surfaces and printed heat exchangers for fusion.
The daily run now also uses technology-first and research searches, still with at most 5 new cards a day.

entries.title: New design, from mood board to Action Radar
entries.summary: ben wasn't keen on the first design. After a mood board and two rounds of concepts he picked the Action Radar, and the new page went live the same evening.
items: Mood board with four looks. ben liked the instrument-panel visuals and the drawing-office styling.
Four new layouts (opportunity map, heat matrix, action radar, spec sheets), then a working preview of all of them on real data, with a clean style, a fifth card-list view, and feedback in every view.
ben chose the Action Radar as the home view, the clean style with light and dark mode, info tooltips, and named comment threads on every card and run.
Built into the real page as PR #2, with a test copy and a "Comment on this finding" button. Merged and live at 21:33.

entries.title: Runs tab and a knowledge base from comments
entries.summary: ben wanted feedback on whole runs and a way to browse old reports, and then for everyone's comments to build up lasting knowledge.
items: A Runs tab lists every run with its frozen report, its own votes and comments, and what it changed from feedback.
Each run reviews feedback before searching. Small changes are made automatically; bigger ones are proposed as P1, P2 and wait for a yes.
Facts from comments ("can't be sold in the UK because of an EU rule") go into a knowledge file that every run reads before scoring.
ben asked Claude to merge PRs for him. The first try was blocked; after ben approved the prompt, PR #1 merged at 21:31.

entries.title: Ideas backlog
entries.summary: ben asked for one place to keep future ideas, with a reminder now and then.
items: The backlog lives in project memory: a monthly digest, research and funding APIs, a wider MTC rollout, MTC data later, patents and US and Asia sources.
A weekly reminder to ben starts on Tuesday 27 October.

entries.title: How Heatmap improves with scale
entries.summary: Reading more articles is the weakest lever: 89% of items already pass the thermal check, and the second batch found half as many new cards per article as the first.
items: Recommended, in order: measure quality first, keep Henry's reading to a short weekly list, choose sources by how much they yield, and keep about 1 card in 5 for exploration.
Structured sources (research papers, UK and EU grants) are where the best information is. ben set up a cloud environment that can reach them.

entries.title: Research and funding APIs tested
entries.summary: UKRI Gateway to Research, CORDIS, arXiv and Crossref all work from the new environment. OpenAlex needs a free key.
items: The grant data was the most useful: Qdot Technology, ToffeeX, Hexxcell, and Reaction Engines with Conflux, each with awards and dates.
CORDIS found new EU projects such as BRIDGE (immersion-cooled data centres, Aalborg University with Heatflow).
Adding these to the daily run is waiting on a yes from ben.

entries.title: Meeting and work log started
entries.summary: ben asked for a running record of meetings with Henry, the work in between, and the action items. This page is the result.
items: The plan for keeping the log up to date is in the linked doc.

entries.title: How a run works explainer
entries.summary: ben asked for a plain-English explainer of a run that he can share with Henry and non-engineers. Three approaches were drafted, and ben picked the worked-example timeline with reference panels.
items: The run at a glance: eight steps from looking to feedback, marking which are done by Claude, the helper program or people.
A real card (DTI's 3D-printed passive chip cooler) followed from search to its score of 86.
Reference panels on sources, topics, searches, scoring, what the AI does, and ground rules.
Corrects one assumption: runs happen in Anthropic's cloud on a schedule, not on ben's desktop.

entries.title: Research and funding APIs added to the daily run
entries.summary: ben added a free OpenAlex key to the environment and said yes to the wiring. Every daily run now also searches five research and funding databases, and the 06:59 run moved to a session that can reach them.
items: Searches UKRI Gateway to Research, CORDIS, OpenAlex, arXiv and Crossref each day. It brings back UK and EU grants with partners, awards and dates, and papers with their institutions.
Once a week it records the recent grants of each UK organisation on a card, for example five for Qdot Technology since 2022.
The 06:59 run now fires in the Research and funding APIs thread. The old scheduled task is paused, not deleted.
The page itself is unchanged. The funding data is stored, ready to show later.

entries.title: First review with Henry
entries.summary: Henry had reviewed the page and was very positive. Over two recorded chats, ben walked him through the work since the kickoff, and they settled how he can use it outside MTC, how to keep his comments safe, and how far to go with customisation.
entries.time_note: The start time wasn't noted. The time shown is when ben posted the notes. The meeting had two recordings: the main discussion, then a walk-through of the log and the page.
discussed: Henry's written feedback before the meeting: the data looks accurate, concise, pertinent and well formatted. His favourite views are the opportunity map, card list and Action Radar.
Henry's asks: more next-step ideas as bullets, confirmation when a comment saves, and a time filter on the opportunity map so it stays usable over months.

Henry's bigger ideas: a short periodic review of whether societal problems are changing (BBC, DTI, ATI, APC, Innovate UK), a front end to tune what each run looks for, suggested new categories that a person approves, and an "I want to know more" button for digging into one card.
Henry can't open the Claude page at work. MTC allows the internet but no AI tools beyond Microsoft Copilot. A plain website he logs into would be like reading a news site.

Grey area: MTC's capabilities and the societal problems are public, but Henry's own specs and comments may count as company knowledge. If he shows it at work it will get a lot of attention, so it has to be watertight.
Longer term: demo it to MTC as built without any internal knowledge, then offer options openly, from MTC owning and self-hosting it with open-source models to a wider tool for its 1,000+ staff.
The daily run's timing is fine while developing (it runs at 06:59 UK; 6 pm was mentioned by mistake). Henry may not keep up with daily runs long term, and missed days of feedback don't matter.
Henry's comments on the page never saved: it held no comments or votes when checked. He most likely had view-only access.

ben walked Henry through the log: the wider sweep, the design options, the Runs tab and knowledge base, the ideas backlog, and the research and funding APIs now in the daily run. Henry liked the "Other" category and all the layouts.
Henry asked how it finds so much that is relevant when MTC's own URL list found little. ben's view: Claude knows where to look, and checks can be added to be sure nothing big is missed.
Ideas for later: flag companies that are MTC members (the list is public), and link to MTC's past work once internal data is allowed.

Dials versus prompts: rather than a settings panel, steer runs with comments on cards, runs, sources and organisations, or with a one-off brief such as "find opportunities for this new fund". Henry thought comments might be enough.
decided: Keep building it outside MTC, just ben and Henry, and focus on making it really good.
Henry must be able to open the page, see the runs and leave comments that Claude can read, using his personal account.
Turn it into a website Henry can log into from any computer, with no AI use on his side.
Keep comments in for now so Henry can give lots of feedback. Add a setting that hides comments, to switch off for a demo.
ben and Henry will be open with MTC about how it was built and offer clear options at a later meeting.
Keep it simple and usable first, and add customisation only where it earns its place.

actions.text: Share the Heatmap page with Henry by email as an Editor, so he can vote and comment.
actions.note: Agreed again in meeting 2: Henry should be able to open the page, see the runs and comment, using his personal account.

actions.text: Leave one test comment on the live page to check your name shows, then delete it.
Give first feedback on the cards (votes, comments, notes), especially aerospace and F1.
actions.note: Henry sent written feedback on the tool before meeting 2. Card-level votes and comments are still to come once he has access.

actions.text: Set up the first-week review with Henry, as the V1 plan suggests.
Say yes or no to adding the research and funding APIs to the daily run and moving the 06:59 run onto the new environment.
Get an OpenAlex key, or tell Claude to request one with your email.
Pick which scaling recommendations to pursue: quality measures, a weekly shortlist, sources by yield, an exploration slot.
Confirm what "I want to count" meant. Claude assumed comment and vote counts and built those.
Delete the merged PR branches on GitHub. Claude can't delete branches from here.
Send a photo of more good and bad examples.
Create the private heatmap repo on GitHub.
Approve the merge prompts for PR #1 and PR #2.
Set up a cloud environment that can reach the research APIs.
Review the run explainer and share it with Henry.
Think through which of your comments and specs might count as MTC knowledge, before showing the tool at work.
